Physics-Inspired Optimizers beyond the Edge of Stability:
Period-Two Orbits and Delayed Instability

Alexander Itin ††thanks: E-mail: alx.itin2@gmail.com; website: AI4science.de Affiliation: Radboud University, Nijmegen, The Netherlands Affiliation: Independent researcher, Hamburg, Germany
Abstract

Gradient descent with momentum can be viewed as a particle that moves with friction in the loss landscape. In deep learning the learning rate is usually large, so training is a discrete dynamical system, not a smooth flow. In many full-batch experiments the sharpness of the loss grows to the stability limit of the optimizer, the edge of stability (EoS), and training continues there, oscillating along the sharpest direction. Physics-inspired optimizers change this motion: Velocity-Regularized Adam (VRAdam), for example, shrinks the step at high speed, motivated by a quartic kinetic energy. We study such methods as kinetic maps, in which the step is the gradient of a kinetic energy of the momentum, and ask what they do beyond the EoS. Our main findings are as follows. (i) In a reduced model, a kinetic map creates a symmetric period-two orbit beyond the edge, where plain momentum diverges. This orbit is strictly linearly stable if and only if the elasticity of the map at its amplitude (the log-log slope of step length versus momentum) lies between 0 and 1; on it, the step reduction exactly compensates the excess sharpness, giving an effective edge of stability. VRAdam’s damper fails this test above twice the critical learning rate, where its kinetic energy is not convex. The Legendre-dual map of VRAdam’s own Lagrangian is convex and passes the test at every learning rate. (ii) Our central dynamical finding is that, because the sharpness rises gradually, the loss of stability is delayed, as in Neishtadt’s theory of slowly swept bifurcations. In a network with a controlled sweep, the measured dynamics match this theory without fitted parameters, including the memory of where the sweep started and its erasure by noise. (iii) Local stability does not guarantee that training reaches the orbit. With momentum, a trajectory can instead end on another attractor, such as a period-four cycle or chaos, unless the map keeps enough elasticity at large momentum; the amount needed grows with the momentum coefficient β1\beta_{1}. Maps that bound the step, such as the relativistic one, already fail at β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9. The cubic-Legendre map (elasticity tending to 1/21/2) reached the orbit from every sampled start up to β1=0.99\beta_{1}=0.99, at the price of an oscillation that grows faster with the learning rate. Experiments support the theory on an exact quadratic problem and in a full-batch MLP, where convex maps hold training near the effective edge while VRAdam’s damper gets stuck at a strongly reduced step. In ResNet-32, maps that act early prevent collapse at large learning rates. On ResNet-18, however, much of the apparent benefit of the maps is reproduced by matching the effective learning rate. Code and data will be made publicly available.

1 Introduction

Gradient descent is one of the oldest algorithms of applied mathematics: Cauchy proposed it in 1847 for astronomical computations (Cauchy, 1847). A century later Polyak added momentum, the heavy ball, by viewing the iteration as a particle that moves with friction in the potential given by the loss (Polyak, 1964), and Nesterov’s acceleration followed (Nesterov, 1983). This mechanical picture has since grown into a theory of its own. For small steps, accelerated methods are discretizations of damped second-order ODEs (Su et al., 2016) and of Bregman–Lagrangian flows (Wibisono et al., 2016), and symplectic integrators discretize such flows (Betancourt et al., 2018). Hamiltonian descent chooses the kinetic energy KK to suit the loss (Maddison et al., 2018), relativistic kinetic energies bound the speed (França et al., 2020), and Lion, Adam and heavy ball can be written as Hamiltonian dynamics with descent and a general kinetic energy (Chen et al., 2024a; Liang et al., 2026). Stochastic gradients add a picture based on modified equations and diffusion (Li et al., 2017).

Deep networks, however, are trained with large steps, and at practical learning rates training is a discrete dynamical system far from its continuous limit. Gradient descent with large constant steps can show period doubling and chaos (Chen et al., 2024b; Kong & Tao, 2020), the route to chaos of the logistic map (Feigenbaum, 1978), and some variable-step variants are chaotic (van den Doel & Ascher, 2012). Large learning rates make networks catapult out of sharp regions (Lewkowycz et al., 2020), and the learning rate in the first phase of training determines the curvature and gradient noise later on (Jastrzebski et al., 2020). Cohen et al. (2021) identified a regime in which full-batch training often operates: the sharpness (the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian) rises until it reaches the stability threshold of the optimizer, 2/η2/\eta for gradient descent, and then stays there, while the iterates oscillate along the top eigenvector and the loss keeps decreasing on average. This edge of stability (EoS) also appears for adaptive methods (Cohen et al., 2022), is maintained by self-stabilization (Damian et al., 2023) and has a stochastic counterpart (Andreyev & Beneventano, 2024). In dynamical-systems terms, the minimum has lost stability through a period-doubling bifurcation, and training proceeds near the period-two orbit born there. We therefore focus on how an optimizer changes this oscillatory regime after the minimum loses stability.

Velocity-Regularized Adam (VRAdam) (Vaidhyanathan et al., 2026) is a recent physics-inspired optimizer. Adding a quartic term β3​v4/4\beta_{3}v^{4}/4 to the kinetic energy of a particle makes its effective mass grow with speed, which suggests damping the learning rate as

ηt=α01+min⁡(β3​‖mt‖2,α1),\eta_{t}=\frac{\alpha_{0}}{1+\min(\beta_{3}\|m_{t}\|^{2},\alpha_{1})}, (1)

where mtm_{t} is Adam’s first moment (written vtv_{t}, a velocity, in VRAdam) and the norm is taken over all parameters. The analysis of VRAdam covers the regime below the EoS threshold, where the damper does not change the linear stability of the minimum. We ask what such kinetic modifications do above the threshold. Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    Period-two orbits, local stability and global attraction (Sections 2.2, 3 and 5). Following the terminology of Hamiltonian descent (Maddison et al., 2018), we call updates u=∇K​(q)u=\nabla K(q) with a radial kinetic energy KK kinetic maps; our results concern their discrete dynamics beyond the stability threshold. With momentum, the symmetric period-two orbit beyond the edge is strictly linearly stable if and only if the elasticity of the map at the orbit lies in (0,1)(0,1) (Theorem 1), and on the orbit the effective step is exactly at the edge, η​λmax​g/aEoS=1\eta\lambda_{\max}g/a_{\mathrm{EoS}}=1 (Corollary 2). VRAdam’s damper is a non-convex member of the family, and its orbit loses stability at twice the threshold step; the Legendre dual of its own Lagrangian is convex and keeps the orbit stable at every step. Whether trajectories reach the orbit depends on how much elasticity the map keeps at large momentum, increasingly so as β1\beta_{1} grows; an exact quadratic problem built from real data reproduces the closed forms to a relative error below 10−710^{-7}.

  2. 2.

    Delayed passage through the edge (Section 4). Because the sharpness rises gradually, the bifurcation is crossed slowly, and the loss of stability is delayed as described by Neishtadt’s theory of dynamical bifurcations. In a network with a controlled sweep, the deviation along the top Hessian direction follows the linear theory without fitted parameters; for slow sweeps the exit point obeys Neishtadt’s entry–exit relation, and noise erases this memory as predicted.

  3. 3.

    Neural-network dynamics and optimizer benchmarks (Sections 6 and 7). In a full-batch MLP the effective-edge law holds and the VR map fails as predicted; in ResNet-32 the orbit forms too late, but maps that act early prevent catapult collapse; with Adam, maps on the preconditioned direction cannot see the amplitude of the oscillation. On ResNet-18, controls with matched effective learning rates remove most of the difference for an Adam map and about half of the gain of Kinetic Muon; the remainder is not resolved by five seeds.

Section 8 discusses connections to capture into resonance, self-organized criticality, ponderomotive forces and feedback control, reports a negative result on grokking, and summarizes limitations and conclusions.

2 Background and kinetic maps

2.1 Related work

Edge of stability.

For gradient descent with step η\eta on a quadratic, the minimum is stable if and only if η​λmax<2\eta\lambda_{\max}<2. With EMA momentum β1\beta_{1} the threshold becomes η​λmax<2​(1+β1)/(1−β1)\eta\lambda_{\max}<2(1+\beta_{1})/(1-\beta_{1}), and for Adam the relevant curvature is the preconditioned sharpness λmax​(P−1​H)\lambda_{\max}(P^{-1}H) with P=diag⁡(s^+ϵ)P=\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{\hat{s}}+\epsilon), which gives 38/η38/\eta at β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9 (Cohen et al., 2021; Cohen et al., 2022). Self-stabilization explains how the oscillation along the top eigenvector reduces the sharpness through third-order terms (Damian et al., 2023); normalized gradient descent was analysed by Arora et al. (2022). Period-two orbits beyond the threshold have been studied in low-dimensional models (Ma et al., 2022; Chen & Bruna, 2023; Zhu et al., 2023; Song & Yun, 2023; Kong & Tao, 2020) and, for gradient descent, derived from a variational functional, with a supercritical bifurcation in two-layer linear networks (Litman, 2026); Wang et al. (2025b) argue, with proofs for a class of nonconvex functions and experiments on networks, that good regularity of the objective makes edge of stability, balancing and catapults more likely at large learning rates. Ma et al. (2022) prove that one-dimensional gradient descent converges to the period-two orbit from almost every start for even losses whose curvature decreases away from the minimum. This global result is stronger than a local analysis; without momentum, our criterion concerns only the linear stability of the orbit. Clipped gradient descent has strictly clipped two-cycles with a unit multiplier (Yuan & Wen, 2026), and Fong & Yang (2026) analyse Adam’s own oscillations. In minibatch training the full-batch sharpness stays below the threshold while a batch sharpness sits at it (Andreyev & Beneventano, 2024); momentum changes this plateau in a way that depends on the batch size (Andreyev et al., 2026). For scale-invariant (normalized) networks, Kodryan et al. (2022) distinguish convergence, chaotic-equilibrium and divergence regimes as the effective learning rate grows, Lobacheva et al. (2021) describe periodic destabilizations under batch normalization and weight decay, and Sadrtdinov et al. (2024) find that the best initial learning rates lie just above the convergence threshold.

Bifurcations in training.

Bifurcations also occur in the dynamics of the trained model itself: in ReLU-based recurrent networks, certain bifurcations of the network’s state-space dynamics crossed during training come with diverging or vanishing gradients and can explain sudden loss jumps (Eisenmann et al., 2023). The bifurcations studied here are of a different kind: they belong to the optimizer map, with the learning rate and the sharpness as parameters.

Kinetic energies in optimization.

Hamiltonian descent (Maddison et al., 2018) matches a kinetic energy to the growth of the objective; relativistic kinetic energies bound the speed (França et al., 2020); Lion-𝒦\mathcal{K} (Chen et al., 2024a) uses a general convex 𝒦\mathcal{K}, and Cautious optimizers (Liang et al., 2026) a general kinetic energy; Karoni et al. (2026) add damping that depends on the kinetic energy. New here are the dynamics beyond the EoS, the elasticity laws, and the identification of VRAdam’s damper as a non-convex member of the family.

Update damping and learning-rate control.

Clipping in various forms suppresses loss spikes (Shazeer & Stern, 2018; Wortsman et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025a; Kumar et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025), and curvature-aware methods set the step from the estimated curvature (Roulet et al., 2024; Malitsky & Mishchenko, 2020). We include a clipping baseline and two curvature controllers.

2.2 Kinetic maps

In Hamiltonian descent, the gradient of a kinetic energy is called a kinetic map (Maddison et al., 2018); we consider radial ones (notation is collected in Table 11). Let qq be the quantity that an optimizer turns into a step (heavy ball: the momentum; Adam: m^/(s^+ϵ)\hat{m}/(\sqrt{\hat{s}}+\epsilon), with s^\hat{s} the second moment). A kinetic map with scale c>0c>0, acting on a block BB of parameters (a tensor, or all parameters), is

uB=ψ⁡(qB)=qB​g​(‖qB‖c),g⁡(0)=1,u_{B}=\psi(q_{B})=q_{B}\,g\!\left(\tfrac{\|q_{B}\|}{c}\right),\qquad g(0)=1, (2)

the gradient of the radial kinetic energy K⁡(q)=k⁡(‖q‖)K(q)=k(\|q\|) with k′​(r)=r​g​(r/c)k^{\prime}(r)=r\,g(r/c). We call gg the step multiplier and ϕ⁡(z)=z​g​(z)\phi(z)=z\,g(z) the radial speed profile, in units of cc. KK is convex if and only if ϕ\phi is non-decreasing. The elasticity of the map is

ε⁡(z)=z​ϕ′​(z)ϕ⁡(z)=d​ln⁡ϕd​ln⁡z.\varepsilon(z)=\frac{z\,\phi^{\prime}(z)}{\phi(z)}=\frac{d\ln\phi}{d\ln z}. (3)

This is the standard elasticity of a function, familiar from economics: the relative change of the speed per relative change of the momentum. A map with ε≡1\varepsilon\equiv 1 does not damp; 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1 means that the speed grows more slowly than the momentum; ε<0\varepsilon<0 (a non-convex KK) means that the speed falls as the momentum grows. Five maps matter here (Fig. 1a,b):

  • •

    VR map ϕ⁡(z)=z/(1+z2)\phi(z)=z/(1+z^{2}): VRAdam’s damper with c=β3−1/2c=\beta_{3}^{-1/2} (ignoring its floor). K=c22​log⁡(1+z2)K=\tfrac{c^{2}}{2}\log(1+z^{2}) is non-convex for z>1z>1, where the speed decreases with momentum.

  • •

    Quartic-Legendre map ϕ=s\phi=s with s+s3=zs+s^{3}=z: the velocity of VRAdam’s own Lagrangian L=12​v2+14​v4L=\tfrac{1}{2}v^{2}+\tfrac{1}{4}v^{4}, obtained by inverting p=∂L/∂vp=\partial L/\partial v. Convex; ε→1/3\varepsilon\to 1/3.

  • •

    Cubic-Legendre map ϕ=s\phi=s with s+s2=zs+s^{2}=z, i.e. s=2​z/(1+1+4​z)s=2z/(1+\sqrt{1+4z}) and g=2/(1+1+4​z)g=2/(1+\sqrt{1+4z}), from L=12​v2+13​|v|3L=\tfrac{1}{2}v^{2}+\tfrac{1}{3}|v|^{3}. Convex; ε→1/2\varepsilon\to 1/2.

  • •

    Relativistic map ϕ⁡(z)=z/1+z2\phi(z)=z/\sqrt{1+z^{2}}, K=c2​1+z2K=c^{2}\sqrt{1+z^{2}} (França et al., 2020): convex, speed bounded by cc, ε→0\varepsilon\to 0.

  • •

    Norm clipping ϕ⁡(z)=min⁡(z,1)\phi(z)=\min(z,1): Huber KK, convex but not strictly; ε=0\varepsilon=0 when clipped.

VRAdam derives the equation of motion v˙=−∇f/(m+3β3v2)\dot{v}=-\nabla f/(m+3\beta_{3}v^{2}) correctly, but then uses 1/(1+β3​v2)1/(1+\beta_{3}v^{2}) as a multiplier of the velocity in the position update. The direct damping rule and the Legendre-dual construction therefore differ in convexity.

4 Delayed passage through the edge

In training, the step is usually fixed while the sharpness rises (progressive sharpening). The bifurcation parameter R=η​λmax/aEoSR=\eta\lambda_{\max}/a_{\mathrm{EoS}} therefore moves slowly through R=1R=1 instead of being fixed. Bifurcations crossed in this way are called dynamical bifurcations. The central result, due to Neishtadt (Neishtadt, 1987; Neishtadt, 1988) and reviewed by Neishtadt & Treschev (2021), is that when a parameter slowly crosses a stability threshold, the system stays near the equilibrium, now unstable, for a long time, of order 1/ρ1/\rho steps for a sweep at rate ρ\rho, before it leaves. We state the linear theory for our map and then test it in a network.

Linear theory.

Near the minimum, a small deviation wt=(yt,vt)w_{t}=(y_{t},v_{t}) of (4) obeys wt+1=J0​(Rt)​wtw_{t+1}=J_{0}(R_{t})\,w_{t}, where J0J_{0} is the Jacobian at the minimum (Appendix A). Let Λ⁡(R)=log⁡r⁡(J0​(R))\Lambda(R)=\log r(J_{0}(R)) be the local growth rate per step, with rr the spectral radius. For b=0.9b=0.9 the eigenvalues of J0J_{0} are complex with modulus b\sqrt{b} for 7×10−4<R<0.99937\times 10^{-4}<R<0.9993, so below the edge

Λ⁡(R)=12​log⁡b=−0.0527,\Lambda(R)=\tfrac{1}{2}\log b=-0.0527, (6)

independent of RR. At R=1R=1 one eigenvalue passes through −1-1 (period doubling), and above the edge Λ\Lambda rises steeply (Λ=0.15\Lambda=0.15 at R=1.01R=1.01 and 0.570.57 at R=1.1R=1.1). If RR changes slowly, Rt=Rin+ρ​tR_{t}=R_{\rm in}+\rho t with ρ≪1\rho\ll 1, the deviation follows the local rate:

|wt|≈C|win|exp⁡(∑s<tΛ⁡(Rs))≈C​|win|​exp⁡(1ρ​∫RinRtΛ⁡(R)​𝑑R),|w_{t}|\;\approx\;C\,|w_{\rm in}|\,\exp\Big(\sum_{s<t}\Lambda(R_{s})\Big)\;\approx\;C\,|w_{\rm in}|\,\exp\Big(\frac{1}{\rho}\int_{R_{\rm in}}^{R_{t}}\Lambda(R)\,dR\Big), (7)

where the factor CC of order one accounts for the slowly turning eigenvectors and for the phase of the rotation below the edge. The deviation shrinks until R=1R=1 and grows afterwards, but it is back at its initial size only when the integral returns to zero. This defines the exit point RoutR_{\rm out} through Neishtadt’s entry–exit relation

∫RinRoutΛ⁡(R)​𝑑R=0.\int_{R_{\rm in}}^{R_{\rm out}}\Lambda(R)\,dR=0. (8)

As ρ→0\rho\to 0 the delay Rout−1R_{\rm out}-1 stays finite. It depends only on where the sweep began, not on ρ\rho or on the size of the deviation: (8) gives Rout=1.080R_{\rm out}=1.080 for Rin=0.5R_{\rm in}=0.5 and 1.1181.118 for Rin=0.1R_{\rm in}=0.1. The contraction accumulated below the edge must be repaid above it. Neishtadt proved that in analytic systems the delay persists even when the equilibrium moves with the parameter (in merely smooth systems it generally does not); in our map the minimum is a fixed point for every RR, so the linear delay carries over directly. For slow passage through a Hopf bifurcation it is known as the memory effect (Baer et al., 1989), and swept period doubling in maps was studied by Kapral & Mandel (1985) and Baesens (1991).

Noise erases the memory.

Now add a forcing ξt\xi_{t} of strength σ\sigma, wt+1=J0​(Rt)​wt+ξtw_{t+1}=J_{0}(R_{t})w_{t}+\xi_{t}, which models minibatch noise, rounding or coupling to the rest of the network. Ignoring the rotation and non-normality of J0J_{0}, the variance of the deviation approximately obeys st+12=e2​Λ​(Rt)​st2+σ2s_{t+1}^{2}=e^{2\Lambda(R_{t})}s_{t}^{2}+\sigma^{2}. Below the edge it settles at the stationary level s∞2≈σ2/(1−b)s_{\infty}^{2}\approx\sigma^{2}/(1-b). Above the edge the deviation grows from this level and reaches a threshold xcx_{c} at

∫1RoutΛ⁡(R)​𝑑R≈ρ​log⁡xcs∞.\int_{1}^{R_{\rm out}}\Lambda(R)\,dR\;\approx\;\rho\,\log\frac{x_{c}}{s_{\infty}}. (9)

The exit then no longer depends on RinR_{\rm in}: the noise has erased the memory. This noise-limited delay grows with the sweep rate ρ\rho and with log⁡(1/σ)\log(1/\sigma), and it vanishes as ρ→0\rho\to 0. A deviation that is still above s∞s_{\infty} when the edge is crossed keeps its memory, so the exit follows (8) for weak noise and (9) for strong noise.

A controlled test in a network.

We impose the sweep in a network; the comparison uses no fitted coefficients, and the linear model is driven by the measured curvature path. We take the tanh MLP of Appendix D (784–128–128–10, MSE loss, 2,000 Fashion-MNIST images) in double precision, pretrain it with full-batch EMA momentum at R=0.5R=0.5 for 1,500 steps, and then set the step at every iteration to ηt=(Rin+ρ​t)​aEoS/λ^t\eta_{t}=(R_{\rm in}+\rho t)\,a_{\mathrm{EoS}}/\hat{\lambda}_{t}, where λ^t\hat{\lambda}_{t} is the latest estimate of λmax\lambda_{\max} from warm-started power iteration, refreshed every five steps; the realized Rt=ηt​λmax​(t)/aEoSR_{t}=\eta_{t}\lambda_{\max}(t)/a_{\mathrm{EoS}} therefore follows the linear ramp only approximately. A second copy of the network starts at θ+δ​u\theta+\delta u, with uu the top Hessian eigenvector, and takes the same steps; no kinetic map is used, and xt=⟨θt(2)−θt(1),ut⟩x_{t}=\langle\theta^{(2)}_{t}-\theta^{(1)}_{t},u_{t}\rangle is the deviation along the top mode. The prediction is the linear recurrence for the top mode in the network’s own coordinates, the displacement xtx_{t} and the corresponding momentum component dtd_{t} (the projection of mt(2)−mt(1)m_{t}^{(2)}-m_{t}^{(1)} on the top eigenvector):

dt+1=b​dt+(1−b)​(λt​xt+ξt),xt+1=xt−ηt​dt+1,d_{t+1}=b\,d_{t}+(1-b)\big(\lambda_{t}x_{t}+\xi_{t}\big),\qquad x_{t+1}=x_{t}-\eta_{t}\,d_{t+1}, (10)

with the steps ηt\eta_{t} actually used, λt\lambda_{t} interpolated linearly between the eigenvalue estimates, the same initial deviation (x0=δx_{0}=\delta, d0=0d_{0}=0) and ξt=0\xi_{t}=0 without injected noise. Changes of the eigenvector between estimates are neglected. This is the exact matrix product of the linear model along the measured path; (7) and (8) are its slow-sweep approximations. In 81 ramps (three seeds, RinR_{\rm in} from 0.10.1 to 0.970.97, ρ\rho from 0.0010.001 to 0.10.1) the network follows the recurrence (10) while the deviation decays by up to 8 orders of magnitude and grows back (Fig. 2a): the largest difference, relative to the local amplitude, is 0.041% in the median run and at most 2% for ρ≥0.003\rho\geq 0.003, and the exit occurs at the same step in network and model in every run. Details, including three excluded runs and the larger errors at ρ=0.001\rho=0.001, are in Appendix C.

The exit point clearly remembers the entry point (Fig. 2b): at ρ=0.003\rho=0.003 a sweep entering at Rin=0.1R_{\rm in}=0.1 leaves at Rout=1.115R_{\rm out}=1.115, one entering at 0.90.9 at 1.0201.020, against 1.1181.118 and 1.0291.029 from (8). For entries up to Rin=0.9R_{\rm in}=0.9 the differences from (8) are at most 0.010 at ρ=0.003\rho=0.003 and 0.004 at ρ=0.001\rho=0.001; they are finite-ρ\rho corrections, which shrink as ρ→0\rho\to 0 and which the model on the measured path reproduces exactly. Adding isotropic gradient noise of standard deviation σ\sigma per coordinate to the second copy (it enters (10) as ξt\xi_{t}, multiplied by 1−b1-b in the momentum; the model distributions are Monte Carlo runs of (10) with the same σ\sigma) erases the memory as predicted (Fig. 2c): with σ=10−9\sigma=10^{-9} the exit still moves with the entry point (from 1.090 to 1.020), with σ=10−7\sigma=10^{-7} it lies at 1.05–1.06 for every entry up to Rin=0.5R_{\rm in}=0.5, and with σ=10−5\sigma=10^{-5} the noise alone is as large as the kick, so the exit comes as soon as the edge is crossed. With noise alone (Fig. 2d) the exit grows with ρ\rho and with log⁡(1/σ)\log(1/\sigma), as (9) predicts; 42 of 45 network exits with kick and noise, and 43 of 45 with noise only, lie within the 10–90% range of the model’s distribution. Near this well-trained state, the network’s top mode behaves almost exactly like the linear two-dimensional map of the theory. The test shows that the delay follows Neishtadt’s mechanism quantitatively; it does not show that the top mode of every network is this linear.

Sweeps in ordinary training.

While the oscillation is still small the kinetic map does not act (g≈1g\approx 1), so Reff=R​gR_{\mathrm{eff}}=Rg follows RR above one until the orbit forms; unless the map is already engaged by the descent momentum, the delay therefore decides how far above the edge the effective step can go. In the reduced model with the cubic map, the peak of ReffR_{\mathrm{eff}} grows with the sweep rate, and the linear theory above predicts it within 3% for ρ<0.01\rho<0.01 (Appendix C). In the networks of Section 6, where the sharpness rises by itself, the overshoot of ResNet-32 grows with the measured sharpening rate (Spearman correlation 0.82 over 15 runs, p=2×10−4p=2\times 10^{-4}), as predicted, but it is larger than the reduced model gives (Fig. 10 in Appendix C); we have not identified what sets its size.

5 Global attraction and an exact quadratic test

5.1 How much elasticity is enough

Theorem 1 is local. Whether a trajectory that starts near the unstable minimum actually reaches the orbit is a global question, and with momentum the answer differs between maps that are locally equivalent. To separate the shape of the map from everything else, we use the Legendre power family: the speed ss solves s+sn=zs+s^{n}=z, which is the velocity of the Lagrangian L=12​v2+1n+1​|v|n+1L=\tfrac{1}{2}v^{2}+\tfrac{1}{n+1}|v|^{n+1} (n=2n=2: cubic, n=3n=3: quartic). Its elasticity decreases from 11 to p=1/np=1/n, and the orbit has the closed form

s∗n−1=A2−1,z∗=s∗​A2,ε∗=A2+n⁡(A−2),s^{\ast\,n-1}=\tfrac{A}{2}-1,\qquad z^{\ast}=s^{\ast}\tfrac{A}{2},\qquad\varepsilon^{\ast}=\frac{A}{2+n(A-2)}, (11)

so every member is locally stable for all A>2A>2. For each β1∈{0,0.5,0.8,0.9,0.95,0.99}\beta_{1}\in\{0,0.5,0.8,0.9,0.95,0.99\}, p∈[0.1,0.67]p\in[0.1,0.67] and A∈{3,…,100}A\in\{3,\dots,100\} (up to 50×50\times the edge step) we iterate (4) from 300 initial conditions (|y0||y_{0}| log-uniform in [10−4,30][10^{-4},30] in units of cc, v0=0v_{0}=0) and record the share that ends on the symmetric orbit (Tables 1 and 3). This share is an empirical attraction fraction under this sampling law, not a two-dimensional basin area.

Observation 6.

(a) Without momentum, every member of the family attracted all sampled initial conditions at every tested step size. (b) With momentum, the worst-case share over step sizes drops sharply when pp falls below a value that grows with β1\beta_{1}: members with p≥1/3p\geq 1/3 keep at least 0.980.98 of the starts for β1≤0.95\beta_{1}\leq 0.95, but at β1=0.99\beta_{1}=0.99 the quartic map keeps only 0.76; members with p≤1/4p\leq 1/4 keep at most 0.48 at β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9 and 0.01 at β1=0.99\beta_{1}=0.99. Only p≥1/2p\geq 1/2 attracted every start in every tested configuration. (c) At β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9 the share depends mainly on the orbit elasticity, across the power, relativistic and log-speed families (Fig. 3a, Fig. 4d): it is at least 0.98 whenever ε∗≥0.34\varepsilon^{\ast}\geq 0.34 and at most 0.32 whenever ε∗<0.25\varepsilon^{\ast}<0.25, with a family-dependent transition in between.

Starts that miss the orbit end on period-four, higher-period or chaotic attractors near the orbit amplitude, or, for a few per cent of the largest starts, on large-amplitude cycles. Saturating maps (ε→0\varepsilon\to 0: relativistic, clipping, log-speed) lose the orbit at moderate steps: the relativistic map keeps at most 0.27 of the starts at β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9 once A≥4A\geq 4. Among the members that were robust everywhere (p≥1/2p\geq 1/2), the cubic-Legendre map damps large momenta the most, and its speed has a closed form. Robustness has a price: on the orbit g⁡(z∗)=2/Ag(z^{\ast})=2/A with g⁡(z)∼zp−1g(z)\sim z^{p-1}, so for large AA and equal cc the amplitude grows as z∗∝A1/(1−p)z^{\ast}\propto A^{1/(1-p)}, i.e. as AA for the relativistic map, A3/2A^{3/2} for the quartic and A2A^{2} for the cubic map (near the edge, for 2<A≲3.72<A\lesssim 3.7, the cubic amplitude is the smallest of the three). These statements hold for the sampling law above, whose upper end exceeds the orbit amplitude |y∗|=z∗/κ|y^{\ast}|=z^{\ast}/\kappa only at small AA and β1\beta_{1} (for the cubic map at A=3A=3, |y∗|=0.75|y^{\ast}|=0.75 in units of cc without momentum, 1414 at β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9 and 149149 at β1=0.99\beta_{1}=0.99); larger starts are discussed in Appendix B.

5.2 An exact quadratic at network scale

To test the theory in high dimension without self-stabilization, we use linear least squares on 2,000 real Fashion-MNIST images (Xiao et al., 2017): L⁡(W)=12​N​‖X​W−Y‖F2L(W)=\tfrac{1}{2N}\|XW-Y\|_{F}^{2} with W∈ℝ785×10W\in\mathbb{R}^{785\times 10} (7,850 parameters, one tensor). The Hessian is C⊗I10C\otimes I_{10}, with λmax=300.4\lambda_{\max}=300.4, and it is constant in time. We use EMA momentum (β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9) with η=μ⋅38/λmax\eta=\mu\cdot 38/\lambda_{\max}, so that A=2​μA=2\mu; the map acts on the tensor norm of the momentum, with cc set to 5%5\% of the initial gradient norm of the first seed (used for all seeds); 6,000 steps, three seeds, 16 values of μ∈[0.5,12]\mu\in[0.5,12].

Plain momentum diverges in all 39/39 runs with μ>1\mu>1. Above the edge, the quartic and cubic maps reach the symmetric orbit in 39/39 and 39/39 runs, with Reff=1R_{\mathrm{eff}}=1 and amplitudes ‖m‖/c\|m\|/c equal to the closed forms of Corollary 3 within relative error 1.7×10−91.7\times 10^{-9} and 3.2×10−83.2\times 10^{-8} (Fig. 4c). The VR map reaches the orbit in 12/15 runs inside its local stability range 1<μ<21<\mu<2 (the others end on coexisting large-amplitude chaotic attractors) and is chaotic beyond it (alternation index 0.11 for μ≥2.25\mu\geq 2.25, against 11 on the orbit). The relativistic map, locally stable everywhere, reached the symmetric orbit in 0/24 runs with μ≥2\mu\geq 2: 17 of them end on a period-four orbit with Reff≈0.5R_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx 0.5 and the rest on other periodic orbits, the failure predicted by Observation 6. Below the edge, 1/18 quartic and cubic runs (quartic, μ=0.9\mu=0.9) ended on a coexisting large-amplitude cycle instead of the minimum, an instance of the large-start caveat.

6 Neural-network dynamics

6.1 Full-batch CIFAR-10 experiments

We train with full-batch EMA momentum on a fixed objective: a balanced 1,000-image CIFAR-10 subset, a tanh MLP (3072–128–128–10, 10 seeds, μ∈{0.5,1,2,4,8}\mu\in\{0.5,1,2,4,8\}) and a ResNet-32 with batch normalization without running statistics, evaluated on four fixed blocks so that the loss is one deterministic function of the parameters (5 seeds, μ∈{0.5,2,4}\mu\in\{0.5,2,4\}). We compute λmax\lambda_{\max} at initialization by Lanczos, set η=μ⋅38/λ0\eta=\mu\cdot 38/\lambda_{0}, and track the top eigenpair and the per-tensor step multipliers. In a network each tensor BB has its own multiplier gBg_{B}, so we measure the effective ratio along the unit top eigenvector uu with the mode-weighted multiplier g¯=∑BgB​‖uB‖2\bar{g}=\sum_{B}g_{B}\|u_{B}\|^{2}:

Reff=R​g¯=R​∑BgB​‖uB‖2,R=η​λmax/aEoS,R_{\mathrm{eff}}=R\,\bar{g}=R\sum_{B}g_{B}\,\|u_{B}\|^{2},\qquad R=\eta\lambda_{\max}/a_{\mathrm{EoS}}, (12)

where uBu_{B} is the part of uu in tensor BB. This is the Rayleigh quotient u⊤​η​G​H​u/aEoSu^{\top}\eta GHu/a_{\mathrm{EoS}} with G=diag⁡(gB)G=\mathrm{diag}(g_{B}); if the top eigenvalue is well separated, it equals the top eigenvalue of η​G​H/aEoS\eta GH/a_{\mathrm{EoS}} to first order in the spread of the multipliers, and it equals R​gR\,g exactly when uu lies in one tensor or when all multipliers are equal. G​HGH is not the full linearization of the update with the map: the derivative of (2) is g⁡(z)g(z) across qq but ϕ′​(z)=g⁡(z)​ε​(z)\phi^{\prime}(z)=g(z)\varepsilon(z) along qq, which is why stability involves the elasticity. Reff≈1R_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx 1 therefore tests the balance of the effective step on the orbit (Corollary 2); it does not by itself measure a Floquet multiplier of the network. We compare plain momentum with the quartic, cubic, relativistic and VR maps at two scales (c=0.05c=0.05 absolute; c=2​‖∇BL​(θ0)‖c=2\|\nabla_{B}L(\theta_{0})\| relative). The questions, fixed before the runs, were whether ReffR_{\mathrm{eff}} is close to one for the convex maps while the sharpness is above the edge, whether the saturating and VR maps fail as predicted, whether the end state returns to R≈1R\approx 1, and how the scale cc matters. We summarize completed runs by their diagnostics with R≥1.1R\geq 1.1 after step 100; these two thresholds were selected after a first inspection of the trajectories, and the summary hardly depends on them (Appendix D). Results on a smaller Fashion-MNIST MLP and the full per-map results are also in Appendix D.

MLP

(450 runs; Fig. 5). Plain momentum diverges in 20/20 runs with μ≥4\mu\geq 4 and in 1/10 at μ=2\mu=2; with the absolute scale, no run with a kinetic map diverged. The convex maps obey the effective-edge law above the plain edge: their points in Fig. 5b lie on the line g¯=1/R\bar{g}=1/R, and over the 178 runs that spend time above the edge the per-run median of ReffR_{\mathrm{eff}} is 1.006 (IQR 1.000–1.018). In the run of Fig. 5a, with the quartic map, the sharpness reaches 1.75×1.75\times the plain edge, and from then on ReffR_{\mathrm{eff}} stays between 0.990.99 and 1.021.02. The VR map behaves as its non-convex profile predicts: it is caught on the branch where a larger momentum gives a smaller step, so its points lie below the line, with Reff=0.64R_{\mathrm{eff}}=0.64 (IQR 0.34–0.87), and the sharpness of the network rises far above the edge (Fig. 5a). In the end the network’s own self-stabilization returns the sharpness to the plain edge, and the multiplier to one, for the quartic and relativistic maps; the map therefore acts during the transient. With the relative scale the maps engage only once the oscillation is large: the open triangles near g¯=1\bar{g}=1 in Fig. 5b are diagnostics at which the map has not yet acted although the sharpness is above the edge. From μ=4\mu=4 on these runs fail, while every map with the absolute scale trains at every μ\mu (Fig. 5c).

ResNet-32

(135 runs; Tables 2 and 6). Here the outcome is decided by whether the map engages before the oscillation grows. At μ≥2\mu\geq 2, plain momentum either diverged (5 of 10 runs) or catapulted towards a nearly constant predictor, ending at losses 0.060–0.090 (predicting the class mean gives 0.090.09). All 40 runs with a map at the absolute scale, the VR map included, trained, and only 2 of the 40 runs at the relative scale did. Unlike in the MLP, the effective-edge law does not describe the ResNet transient: the sharpness rises above the edge and falls back within one or two hundred steps, too fast for the oscillation to form (Section 4). In this network the map works as an early brake on the descent momentum, not as a regulator of the edge oscillation.

6.2 Adam: maps on the preconditioned direction

For Adam, a kinetic map can act on the preconditioned direction q=m^/(s^+ϵ)q=\hat{m}/(\sqrt{\hat{s}}+\epsilon) or on the raw first moment m^\hat{m}. The two differ at the edge:

Proposition 7 (Preconditioned maps are amplitude-blind).

Let a coordinate of the gradient alternate as ∇t=(−1)t​Y\nabla_{t}=(-1)^{t}Y for longer than the second-moment memory 1/(1−β2)1/(1-\beta_{2}). Then Adam’s m^t→±κ​Y\hat{m}_{t}\to\pm\kappa Y and s^t→Y\sqrt{\hat{s}_{t}}\to Y, so qt→±κY/(Y+ϵ)q_{t}\to\pm\kappa\,Y/(Y+\epsilon) with κ=(1−β1)/(1+β1)\kappa=(1-\beta_{1})/(1+\beta_{1}): independent of YY for ϵ=0\epsilon=0, and approximately so for Y≫ϵY\gg\epsilon.

In this stationary limit a map on the preconditioned direction applies an attenuation that does not depend on the amplitude: it can change the oscillation, but it cannot provide feedback on its absolute size, and it reacts only to amplitude changes faster than 1/(1−β2)1/(1-\beta_{2}) steps. A map on the raw first moment (in absolute units, as in VRAdam) retains that information. We compare both in full-batch Adam on the ResNet-32 objective of Section 6. With relativistic maps on rms⁡(qB)\mathrm{rms}(q_{B}) and on ‖m^B‖\|\hat{m}_{B}\| (Table 3; three seeds, η∈{0.002,0.01}\eta\in\{0.002,0.01\}), all 24 runs end at the adaptive edge (late preconditioned RR between 0.91 and 1.00), and none diverges. The maps act early, while the descent momentum is large (smallest multiplier in the first 100 steps: 0.12–0.15 for the map on m^\hat{m}, 0.10–0.60 for VRAdam; the map on qq starts at 0.45 because q=±1q=\pm 1 at the first step), and they are essentially inactive at the edge: in the second half of training the smallest multiplier is 0.99 for the map on m^\hat{m} and 1.00 for VRAdam. Adam’s edge oscillation is therefore small in absolute units, whereas the map on qq still reacts to transients (down to 0.61), as Proposition 7 implies.

In minibatch training with Adam (ResNet-32, batch 1,000), the preconditioned sharpness of the training batch stays well below the full-batch threshold, while a preconditioned batch sharpness scales as 1/η1/\eta, consistent with dynamics limited by stochastic stability (Andreyev & Beneventano, 2024); see Appendix D.

7 Optimizer benchmarks and effective-rate controls

Algorithm 1 adds one reduction per tensor to AdamW; with g≡1g\equiv 1 it is AdamW exactly. The map can wrap any optimizer in update space; we also use it on Muon. Proposition 7 favours a map on the raw first moment; in the CNN, character-level and ResNet-18 benchmarks below, the Kinetic Adam variants act on qq (with a fixed or an EMA scale), and in the GPT and grokking studies on m^\hat{m}.

Benchmarks.

With an equal tuning budget (10 random-search trials per method, three fresh seeds; Appendix E), every Adam variant with a fixed scale, VRAdam and the preconditioned curvature controller end close to AdamW (test loss 0.2660.266–0.2800.280 against 0.275±0.0040.275\pm 0.004 on a Fashion-MNIST CNN, and 1.701.70–1.741.74 on a character-level transformer), and Muon with a quartic map ends close to Muon (0.2590.259 against 0.2610.261 on the CNN). VRAdam’s one distinct advantage is at very large learning rates: on an MLP it is the only method that still learns at about 30×30\times AdamW’s best learning rate (Fig. 12 in Appendix E). This is consistent with braking on the absolute momentum magnitude (Proposition 7), not from velocity dynamics.

ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 with effective-learning-rate controls.

After a random search (Appendix E), Kinetic Muon had the highest accuracy, and the quartic Adam variants raised accuracy but also cross-entropy relative to AdamW, consistent with a larger effective step. We therefore reran the selected configurations next to controls with matched effective learning rates (Table 4; 5 seeds shared by all rows, so differences are paired). These are the seeds of the tuned comparison, so the tuned rows repeat those runs up to non-deterministic GPU arithmetic and are not an independent replication. Kinetic Muon beats tuned Muon, by +0.17±0.13+0.17\pm 0.13 pp accuracy and −0.016±0.011-0.016\pm 0.011 cross-entropy (p=0.04p=0.04 and 0.030.03, paired tt-test). Against Muon run at Kinetic Muon’s effective learning rates, the differences shrink to +0.10±0.20+0.10\pm 0.20 pp and −0.009±0.015-0.009\pm 0.015 (95% intervals -0.15 to +0.34 pp and -0.028 to +0.010; p=0.33p=0.33, 0.280.28); in point estimate, the change of learning rate alone gives about half of the cross-entropy difference (−0.008-0.008, p=0.07p=0.07). For Adam, the global quartic map is not resolved from AdamW at three times its tuned learning rate (+0.05+0.05 pp, +0.008+0.008 cross-entropy, p>0.17p>0.17). Matching the effective learning rates thus removes most of the difference for the Adam map and, in point estimate, about half of it for Kinetic Muon; the remaining differences are not resolved by five seeds, so these experiments support a substantial learning-rate contribution without establishing equivalence. All pp-values are unadjusted paired tt-tests for the comparisons the controls were designed for.

Small GPT.

In a 51.5M-parameter GPT-2-style model trained on FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., 2024) (Appendix E), every method is best at the same learning rate, where the final validation losses of AdamW, clipping, VRAdam and the cubic map span only 0.032 nats, against a spread of 0.026 over initialization seeds for AdamW. At about three times that learning rate AdamW fails, clipping largely avoids the failure, the cubic map partly does, and VRAdam does not. With two seeds per setting, no kinetic map improves the best loss beyond seed noise or extends the usable range of learning rates beyond what clipping does.

8 Discussion and conclusions

8.1 Connections to nonlinear dynamics

The edge of stability is a phenomenon of nonlinear dynamics, and Section 4 applied one classical result to it. Here we note further connections to nonlinear dynamics and report a test on grokking.

Weak dissipation and capture into resonance.

The one-step Jacobian of (4) has determinant b=β1b=\beta_{1} everywhere. In the variables (v,u)(v,u) with u=(1−b)​yu=(1-b)y the map reads v′=b​v+uv^{\prime}=bv+u, u′=u−(1+b)​A​ϕ​(v′)u^{\prime}=u-(1+b)A\,\phi(v^{\prime}); as β1→1\beta_{1}\to 1 at fixed AA it becomes a weakly dissipative perturbation of the area-preserving map v′=v+uv^{\prime}=v+u, u′=u−2​A​ϕ​(v′)u^{\prime}=u-2A\,\phi(v^{\prime}), and the symmetric orbit becomes a weakly damped elliptic point (Appendix A). In area-preserving maps, elliptic points are surrounded by chains of resonance islands, and weak dissipation can turn islands into competing attractors. Which attractor a trajectory reaches is then expected to be a problem of capture into resonance, as in slowly varying or weakly dissipative Hamiltonian systems, where capture probabilities are set by phase-space fluxes (Neishtadt, 1975; Arnold et al., 2006) and, for maps with a constant Jacobian, by the areas of the islands (Chirikov & Izraelev, 1981; Lieberman & Tsang, 1985). Capture into resonance governs, for example, the acceleration of charged particles by waves (Itin et al., 2000; Itin, 2002; Neishtadt et al., 2011; Artemyev et al., 2018), the destruction of adiabatic invariance in slowly perturbed elliptic billiards (Itin & Neishtadt, 2003), Fermi acceleration in time-dependent rectangular billiards (Itin & Neishtadt, 2012) and resonant phenomena in the classical three-body Coulomb problem (Itin, 2003). We expect the period-four and higher-period attractors of Section 5 to be of this kind, and the growth with β1\beta_{1} of the elasticity required for global attraction to reflect the weaker dissipation; a quantitative treatment is left for future work.

Averaged force.

Averaging the loss over a period-two oscillation of amplitude δ\delta along the top eigenvector uu gives 12​[L⁡(θ+δ​u)+L⁡(θ−δ​u)]=L⁡(θ)+12​δ2​λ​(θ)+O⁡(δ4)\tfrac{1}{2}[L(\theta+\delta u)+L(\theta-\delta u)]=L(\theta)+\tfrac{1}{2}\delta^{2}\lambda(\theta)+O(\delta^{4}): the fast oscillation exerts a force −12δ2∇λ-\tfrac{1}{2}\delta^{2}\nabla\lambda on the slow variables and pushes them towards lower sharpness. This is the averaged form of self-stabilization (Damian et al., 2023), analogous to the ponderomotive force and to Kapitza’s pendulum, where a fast vibration creates an effective potential for the slow motion (Kapitza, 1951; Landau & Lifshitz, 1976). A kinetic map sets δ\delta, and hence the strength of this force (Appendix B).

Other analogies.

The EoS has the structure of self-organized criticality (Bak et al., 1987), with progressive sharpening as the slow drive and catapults and self-stabilization as the fast relaxation; Katsnelson et al. (2021) argue that learning dynamics are generically attracted to such a critical state, and in this language a kinetic map moves the critical point from η​λ=aEoS\eta\lambda=a_{\mathrm{EoS}} to η​λ​g=aEoS\eta\lambda g=a_{\mathrm{EoS}}. A kinetic map is also a governor on the optimizer’s speed, in the sense of Maxwell’s analysis of feedback control (Maxwell, 1868): a convex map throttles less than proportionally, whereas VRAdam’s non-convex map throttles more than proportionally beyond z=1z=1, so that a larger drive gives a smaller speed. Finally, for networks with normalization layers Kodryan et al. (2022) find convergence, chaotic-equilibrium and divergence regimes as the effective learning rate grows, and Lobacheva et al. (2021) describe periodic destabilizations under weight decay; the reduced model has analogous regimes, and with the convex maps we tested (g∞=0g_{\infty}=0) the divergence regime of plain momentum is replaced by bounded oscillations.

Grokking.

Networks trained on small algorithmic tasks can generalize long after fitting the training set (Power et al., 2022; Nanda et al., 2023). With adaptive optimizers this late generalization coincides with norm growth and loss spikes (“slingshots”) (Thilak et al., 2022), and Prieto et al. (2025) relate grokking to numerical instability, so edge-of-stability dynamics could be involved. Clipping and kinetic maps on m^\hat{m} can damp such spikes, which gives a direct test: if the spikes drove grokking, damping them should delay it. In modular addition with weight decay (Appendix F), clipping and the cubic map with k=1k=1 lowered the median of the largest training loss after memorization about fourfold (not on every seed) without a significant delay of grokking, and larger spikes did not go with earlier grokking. Conclusion: in this setting, reducing the measured loss peaks did not consistently delay grokking, and the large spikes seen without weight decay did not produce it; with three seeds per method we see no significant effect of the maps on when grokking occurs. Beyond this negative result we found no link between grokking and the mechanisms studied here.

8.2 Limitations

The reduced model freezes Adam’s preconditioner; minibatch noise, the scale invariance of batch-normalized networks and the large-amplitude cycles reachable from large starts are outside the theorem, and Observation 6 is numerical, not proved. In nonlinear networks the sharpness self-stabilizes to the plain edge (except with the cubic map in our MLP, which ends above it, at RR up to 3.32 for μ≥1\mu\geq 1), so the orbit theory governs the transient, not the end state. The basin results are for sampled initial conditions on a grid of step sizes and momentum values, and the robustness of the cubic map is a statement about the reduced model: in the MLP it trained worse than the quartic and relativistic maps. The controlled delay test was run near a well-trained state, where the top mode is linear to high accuracy; in ordinary ResNet-32 training the overshoot follows the predicted trend but is larger than the reduced model gives. In ResNet-32 the transient is too fast for the orbit to form, so maps at the absolute scale help there as early brakes, not through the effective-edge law. As optimizers, kinetic maps were within noise of tuned baselines on our small benchmarks, and on ResNet-18 controls with matched effective learning rates reproduce most of the effect of an Adam map and about half of the gain of Kinetic Muon, with the remainder not resolved by five seeds.

8.3 Recommendations

(i) Use a convex map, and choose its elasticity knowing the trade-off: a high asymptotic elasticity (cubic, p=1/2p=1/2) gave the most reliable attraction to the orbit in the reduced model, a low one a smaller oscillation at large steps; in our MLP at μ≥1\mu\geq 1 the quartic and relativistic maps trained better than the cubic one, while in ResNet-32 the differences were small. (ii) Apply the map per tensor and to the raw first moment. (iii) Choose cc small enough that the map engages before the oscillation grows: it sets the oscillation amplitude, and in our MLP study a scale relative to the initial gradient norm engaged too late. (iv) Report step multipliers and effective learning rates with any comparison.

8.4 Conclusions

We have analysed how kinetic maps change momentum dynamics after a minimum loses stability. In the reduced model, the elasticity of the speed profile gives an exact criterion for the local stability of the symmetric period-two orbit, and on that orbit the step multiplier compensates exactly for the excess curvature. VRAdam’s damper violates this criterion from twice the edge step on, while the Legendre-dual map of its own Lagrangian satisfies it at every step. Numerical basin experiments show that the local result does not determine which attractor a trajectory reaches: with heavy momentum this also requires elasticity at large momentum.

Our central dynamical result concerns the gradual passage through the edge. In controlled network experiments, the linear recurrence on the measured curvature path reproduces the delayed loss of stability without fitted parameters, and the exit points follow the entry–exit relation of Neishtadt’s theory of slowly swept bifurcations, including the dependence on the entry point and its suppression by noise. In ordinary full-batch training the overshoot grows with the sharpening rate, as predicted, but it is larger than the reduced model gives, and we have not identified what sets its size.

These dynamical results do not imply a general improvement in predictive performance. In networks the map acts in two different ways: it holds a settled oscillation at the effective edge (MLP), or it brakes the early descent (ResNet-32). On ResNet-18, controls with matched effective learning rates reproduce much of the apparent gains: most of the difference for an Adam map and about half of it for Kinetic Muon. Separating these mechanisms, and stating where each explanation is supported, is a main aim of this work. The weakly dissipative limit β1→1\beta_{1}\to 1, in which capture into resonance should decide which attractor training reaches, is left for future work.

Appendix B Additional results for the reduced model

Large starts.

The basin statements of Section 5 hold for the sampling law stated there, whose starts are mostly smaller than the orbit (at most 29%29\% of them exceed |y∗||y^{\ast}|, at β1=0\beta_{1}=0 and A=3A=3), as for trajectories that leave the minimum as it loses stability. Larger starts can lock into large-amplitude cycles for every map we tested: for the cubic map the smallest such start on a logarithmic grid lies between 0.5 and 4.4 times the orbit amplitude |y∗||y^{\ast}| (β1∈{0.9,0.99}\beta_{1}\in\{0.9,0.99\}, A∈{3,6,20}A\in\{3,6,20\}).

Global versus per-block maps.

Figure 8 illustrates Proposition 5 on a block-diagonal quadratic.

Amplitude-controlled self-stabilization.

The map bounds the oscillation instead of removing it. In the model of Damian et al. (2023), f=12​(S0+γ​w)​x2f=\tfrac{1}{2}(S_{0}+\gamma w)x^{2}, the oscillation amplitude is c​z∗​(A)c\,z^{\ast}(A) and the sharpness decreases at a rate ∝c2\propto c^{2} (measured slopes 1.921.92, 1.961.96, 2.002.00 for the quartic, relativistic and VR maps; Fig. 9). This is the averaged force of Section 8.1. The VR map stalls: beyond its stable range the iterate spends long stretches at large momenta where ϕ\phi is small, and the sharpness stays far above the edge (S=4.79S=4.79 against ≈2\approx 2).

Appendix C Delayed loss of stability: details

Controlled ramps.

We ran 84 ramps. At the slowest rate we also tracked the reference trajectory along uu, and we exclude the 3 runs at ρ=0.001\rho=0.001 and Rin=0.5R_{\rm in}=0.5, in which the reference trajectory’s own period-two oscillation, driven by training itself, grows to the size of the kick before the kicked deviation returns. At ρ=0.001\rho=0.001 the largest difference between network and model reaches 25%, near the bottom of the decay just below the edge; in a test run (seed 2, Rin=0.7R_{\rm in}=0.7) it fell from 25% to 8.7% with a kick of 10−610^{-6} instead of 10−410^{-4}, and to 1.9% when the sharpness was also tracked at every step instead of every fifth, with the same exit point in all three cases. The sharpness itself drifts by up to 9.5% during a ramp. At faster sweeps the exit also depends on the phase of the rotation below the edge at the moment of crossing, so that RoutR_{\rm out} varies non-monotonically with RinR_{\rm in}; the model reproduces this run by run. On an exact linear ramp (thin lines in Fig. 2b) the model differs from the network by up to 0.009, because the imposed ramp is only approximately linear. For entries closer to the edge than Rin=0.9R_{\rm in}=0.9 the kick has barely decayed when the edge is crossed, and its transient growth below the edge (by a factor of three to five, since the linear map is not normal) decides the exit. In the runs with noise, the count of exits within the model’s 10–90% range includes runs at σ=10−5\sigma=10^{-5} in which both exit on the first step past the edge. Sharpness and loss after pretraining: 206–211 and 0.015–0.017.

Reduced model with a kinetic map.

With a map, the exit leads onto the period-two orbit, and ReffR_{\mathrm{eff}} returns to one once the orbit has formed. Propagating the amplitude variance st+12=e2​Λ​(Rt)​st2+σ2s_{t+1}^{2}=e^{2\Lambda(R_{t})}s_{t}^{2}+\sigma^{2} predicts when the amplitude reaches the orbit. We sweep RR linearly from 0.50.5 at rate ρ\rho per step in the reduced model with the cubic map and β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, starting from a deviation 10−3​c10^{-3}c with forcing σ\sigma (Fig. 10). The peak of ReffR_{\mathrm{eff}} grows with ρ\rho. For slow sweeps the deviation decays to the noise floor before the crossing, and the overshoot decreases logarithmically as the noise grows; for fast sweeps it is set by the initial deviation. The linear estimate, taken as the RR at which the propagated amplitude reaches half the orbit amplitude, follows the simulation within 3% for ρ<0.01\rho<0.01 and overestimates the peak by up to 24% at the fastest rates.

Sweeps in the networks of Section 6.

For every run at μ=0.5\mu=0.5 with plain momentum or a convex map at the absolute scale, we measure the sharpening rate at the crossing (a chord between the two diagnostics around R=1R=1) and the largest ReffR_{\mathrm{eff}} while the sharpness climbs (Fig. 10b). In ResNet-32 the overshoot grows with the sharpening rate (Spearman correlation 0.82 over 15 runs, p=2×10−4p=2\times 10^{-4}): the 9 runs that cross at ρ≥0.04\rho\geq 0.04 per step peak at Reff=2.0R_{\mathrm{eff}}=2.0–3.6, the 6 slower ones at most at 1.17. In the MLP, plain momentum crosses at ρ≲0.010\rho\lesssim 0.010 and overshoots by at most a factor 1.06. The reduced model reproduces this trend but not its size: 11 of the 15 ResNet peaks lie above the range it gives over initial amplitudes from 10−610^{-6} to 11. In the MLP a map is already engaged by the large descent momentum before the crossing: with the quartic map, ReffR_{\mathrm{eff}} is 0.55 at the crossing (seed 0) and at most 1.00 during the climb to R=1.75R=1.75.

Appendix D Networks: additional results

Fashion-MNIST MLP.

With a tanh MLP (784–128–128–10, MSE, 2,000 images, one seed), plain momentum diverges for μ≥2\mu\geq 2. For μ∈{2,4}\mu\in\{2,4\} every map, the VR map included, trains, and every run ends with R=η​λmax/aEoS∈[0.99,1.01]R=\eta\lambda_{\max}/a_{\mathrm{EoS}}\in[0.99,1.01] (Fig. 11): the network’s sharpness self-stabilizes down to the plain edge, where the multiplier returns to one. At μ=8\mu=8 with a common c=0.05c=0.05 only the VR map reached a low loss; with cc chosen per map (Fig. 11c) all maps reach losses between 3.7×10−53.7\times 10^{-5} and 1.5×10−41.5\times 10^{-4}, the quartic map needing the smallest cc (0.005). The oscillation amplitude scales with cc, so in networks cc trades the size of the edge oscillation against the large-start risk of Section 5.

MLP on CIFAR-10: details.

To summarize the transient we take, for every completed run, the median of ReffR_{\mathrm{eff}} over the Lanczos diagnostics with R≥1.1R\geq 1.1 after step 100; these two thresholds were chosen after a first look at the data. For thresholds R≥1.05R\geq 1.05, 1.11.1, 1.21.2 or 1.51.5 and steps ≥50\geq 50, 100100 or 200200, the median over runs of this per-run median stays between 1.004 and 1.009 for the convex maps (114–213 runs contribute) and between 0.62 and 0.71 for the VR map. The Lanczos estimates converged at all diagnostics, and the two independent starts used for calibration agree to <10−4<10^{-4}. With the absolute scale no run with a kinetic map diverged (0/200); 96% of the convex-map runs have a per-run median ReffR_{\mathrm{eff}} within ±10%\pm 10\% of one. During the climb itself ReffR_{\mathrm{eff}} lags behind (0.800.80 at R=1.38R=1.38 in the run of Fig. 5a), and pooled over individual diagnostics rather than runs, 93%93\% (absolute scale) and 75%75\% (relative scale) of the points lie within ±10%\pm 10\% of one. The VR map’s lowest values come from the relative scale; with the absolute scale and μ≤1\mu\leq 1 it ends at R=4.7R=4.7 with a final loss 316 times that of plain momentum. The differences between convex maps predicted by the reduced model (relativistic versus quartic) do not appear in the network. For μ≥1\mu\geq 1, all completed runs with the quartic or relativistic map and the absolute scale end within 1%1\% of R=1R=1 (40/40 and 40/40). With the relative scale, 12/20 quartic and 6/20 relativistic runs with μ≥4\mu\geq 4 diverged, and the VR map does not diverge but ends at losses of 7–41 at μ=8\mu=8, against an initial 0.6; here the quartic map fails more often than the relativistic one, the opposite of the reduced model’s ranking. Where plain momentum is stable (μ≤1\mu\leq 1), the maps with the absolute scale only slow training (quartic: 13 times the final loss of plain momentum).

The cubic map holds the effective step at the edge most tightly (per-run median Reff=1.003R_{\mathrm{eff}}=1.003, IQR 1.000–1.006, absolute scale), but it trains worse than the quartic and relativistic maps (Table 5) and, unlike them, does not return to the plain edge: for μ≥1\mu\geq 1 it ends at R=1.01R=1.01–3.32 (within 1%1\% of one: cubic 0/40, quartic 40/40, relativistic 40/40), and at μ=8\mu=8 its median final loss is 0.20 against 3.1×10−63.1{\times}10^{-6} (quartic) and 1.9×10−71.9{\times}10^{-7} (relativistic). At μ=8\mu=8 this is consistent with the faster growth of the cubic orbit amplitude (Section 5); at μ≤4\mu\leq 4, where the cubic runs end at R≈1.02R\approx 1.02–1.121.12, the closed forms give the cubic map the smallest amplitude, so amplitude does not explain the gap there. A plausible cause is the shape of the multiplier near zero speed: the cubic map’s falls off linearly, g≈1−zg\approx 1-z, because |v|3|v|^{3} is not analytic at 00, whereas the quartic, relativistic and VR multipliers fall off quadratically, so any residual momentum keeps the cubic multiplier below one and the sharpness above the plain edge. With the relative scale the cubic map diverged in 19/20 runs with μ≥4\mu\geq 4.

ResNet-32: details.

Plain momentum at μ≥2\mu\geq 2 that did not diverge catapulted: its sharpness fell to 0.010–0.10 of the edge, towards a nearly constant predictor (5 runs). All runs with a map at the absolute scale trained with final loss at most 2.7×10−42.7{\times}10^{-4}; at the relative scale 28 runs collapsed, 9 diverged and one ended at 0.0160.016. At μ=0.5\mu=0.5 every run trained. Over the few diagnostics above the plain edge, the per-run median of ReffR_{\mathrm{eff}} is 1.363 (IQR 1.215–1.578; 37 runs). Neither the convexity nor the elasticity of the map plays a visible role in preventing the collapse (at μ=0.5\mu=0.5 the VR and relativistic maps at the absolute scale do end at higher losses, Fig. 6c).

Minibatch curvature.

In an earlier minibatch ResNet-32 study (batch 1,000, Adam), the preconditioned sharpness sat at R≈0.2R\approx 0.2–0.30.3 for every learning rate between 10−310^{-3} and 10−210^{-2}, i.e. it scaled as 1/η1/\eta but stayed far below the full-batch threshold. Two explanations are possible: an estimator biased low by the large negative spectral tail of batch-normalized networks (at initialization λmin≈−57​λmax\lambda_{\min}\approx-57\lambda_{\max}, which slows shifted power iteration), or the edge of stochastic stability, where a batch sharpness rather than λmax\lambda_{\max} sits at the threshold (Andreyev & Beneventano, 2024). We repeated the setting (16 runs: two seeds, β2∈{0.95,0.999}\beta_{2}\in\{0.95,0.999\}, four learning rates; Table 6) with Lanczos (full re-orthogonalization; converged when the a-posteriori bound r2/(θ1−θ2)r^{2}/(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}) on the error of the top Ritz value θ1\theta_{1}, with residual rr and Ritz gap θ1−θ2\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}, falls below 2×10−3​θ12\times 10^{-3}\theta_{1} and θ1\theta_{1} has changed by less than 10−3​θ110^{-3}\theta_{1} over the last eight iterations, or when r<10−2​θ1r<10^{-2}\theta_{1}; this criterion was met at every diagnostic, but the Ritz gap only estimates the true spectral gap), the earlier power iteration and the preconditioned batch sharpness on the same batches. Late in training, the preconditioned sharpness of the training batch is R=0.16R=0.16–0.27 by Lanczos, and the earlier estimate is 0.87–1.00 of it: the low values are real, not an estimator artefact (the negative tail has shrunk to λmin/λmax=−0.11\lambda_{\min}/\lambda_{\max}=-0.11 to -0.06). The preconditioned batch sharpness, λbs=∑k(P−1​∇k)⊤​Hk​(P−1​∇k)/∑k∇k⊤P−1​∇k\lambda_{\rm bs}=\sum_{k}(P^{-1}\nabla_{k})^{\top}H_{k}(P^{-1}\nabla_{k})\big/\sum_{k}\nabla_{k}^{\top}P^{-1}\nabla_{k} over K=4K=4 fresh augmented batches kk with gradients ∇k\nabla_{k} and Hessians HkH_{k} and the current preconditioner P=diag⁡(s^+ϵ)P=\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{\hat{s}}+\epsilon) (a ratio of sums), is η​λbs=2.8\eta\lambda_{\rm bs}=2.8–4.3 (Rbs=0.073R_{\rm bs}=0.073–0.112) across a tenfold range of learning rates, i.e. it scales as 1/η1/\eta, as at an edge, at a level well below the full-batch adaptive threshold 38/η38/\eta. This is consistent with dynamics limited by stochastic stability (Andreyev & Beneventano, 2024), but these experiments do not establish the corresponding stability boundary for Adam. For SGD with heavy-ball momentum, Andreyev et al. (2026) find batch-sharpness plateaus below the full-batch threshold; Adam’s preconditioned version, which their analysis does not cover, plateaus here at η​λbs≈3\eta\lambda_{\rm bs}\approx 3–44.

Appendix E Optimizer benchmarks: additional results

Equal-budget comparisons.

These small models were trained on CPU. Every method receives 10 random-search trials over its own hyperparameters, selected by validation loss, and then three fresh seeds on held-out data (Table 7; search spaces in Appendix G). For the CNN, validation uses 5,000 of the 10,000 training images held out from training, and test the first 5,000 test images; for the character-level model, both losses are computed on 64 random windows of 64 characters from the same held-out last 10%10\% of the text, so validation and test are not disjoint there. On a Fashion-MNIST CNN, every Adam variant with a fixed scale, VRAdam and the preconditioned controller reach test losses of 0.2660.266–0.2800.280, against AdamW’s 0.275±0.0040.275\pm 0.004, while the EMA-scale variant and the directional controller are clearly worse; Muon and Muon with a quartic map are best (0.2610.261, 0.2590.259). On a character-level transformer the same Adam variants lie within 1.701.70–1.741.74, the EMA-scale variant fails (2.062.06), and Muon (1.59±0.011.59\pm 0.01) is clearly better than everything else. On an MLP, VRAdam is the only method that still learns at η=0.1\eta=0.1, about 30×30\times AdamW’s best learning rate (validation loss 0.910.91–1.011.01 over two seeds, against 2.302.30 at chance for all others; Fig. 12).

ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10: tuned comparison.

Twelve random-search trials per method (30 epochs, selection by validation cross-entropy on a held-out split of 5k images), then five fresh seeds for 50 epochs evaluated on the test set (batch 512, bf16, cosine schedule, weight decay 5×10−45\times 10^{-4}, which the Muon variants apply to all tensors and the Adam variants only to tensors with at least two dimensions; Table 8). Kinetic Muon has the highest mean accuracy and a lower cross-entropy than Muon (paired over seeds: −0.011±0.006-0.011\pm 0.006 CE, +0.17±0.11+0.17\pm 0.11 pp; the reruns with the same seeds in Table 4 give −0.016-0.016 and +0.17+0.17 pp, a measure of the variation from non-deterministic GPU arithmetic); the quartic Adam variants raise accuracy but also cross-entropy relative to AdamW. The selected configurations differ in effective learning rate: Kinetic Muon’s EMA map settles at a multiplier of 0.660.66 in these runs, which places it at 1.8×1.8\times Muon’s learning rate for the Muon-updated parameters and 0.08×0.08\times for the Adam-updated ones. These differences motivated the controls of Table 4, in which the multiplier measured was 0.70, slightly above the 0.660.66 used to set the controls, so the controls match the effective learning rates only approximately; there, both the quartic map and AdamW at three times its tuned learning rate raise accuracy by about half a point and cross-entropy by 0.020.02–0.030.03 relative to tuned AdamW, which was selected for cross-entropy. The two curvature controllers estimate the sharpness with Hessian-vector products; in this study those extra forward passes ran in training mode and therefore also updated the batch-normalization running statistics used at test time. Their test numbers may be affected in either direction, and we report them for completeness only.

Small GPT.

A 51.5M-parameter GPT-2-style model (8 layers, width 512, context 1,024) trained for 6,000 steps of 64×1,02464\times 1{,}024 tokens on FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., 2024), with AdamW, AdamW with gradient clipping at 1.01.0, VRAdam, and AdamW with the cubic map on m^\hat{m} at two scales, over learning rates 10−310^{-3}–3×10−23\times 10^{-2} and two seeds (40 runs, 393M tokens each, about 16 minutes per run on one A100; Tables 9 and 13). The data are the first file of the sample-10BT subset, tokenized with the GPT-2 tokenizer; its first 1010M tokens (whole documents) are held out for validation and the following tokens are used for training. For the maps, cB=k​rms​(m^B)c_{B}=k\,\mathrm{rms}(\hat{m}_{B}) is frozen at the end of the 300-step warm-up. The data order is the same in every run, and the two seeds change only the initialization, which is shared across methods. Every method is best at η=0.003\eta=0.003, where the mean final validation losses span only 0.032 nats (AdamW 3.714, clipping 3.716, VRAdam 3.705, cubic map 3.706 with k=4k=4 and 3.737 with k=1k=1), against a spread over initialization seeds of 0.026 for AdamW. The maps act as learning-rate reductions there (mean multiplier 0.54 for k=1k=1 and 0.78 for k=4k=4; VRAdam’s factor is 1.00). At η=0.01\eta=0.01 AdamW fails (6.47 and 6.69), clipping largely avoids the failure (3.79 and 4.07, against its best of 3.716), the cubic map with k=1k=1 partly does, with a large seed dependence (3.96 and 4.84), and VRAdam does not (5.99 and 6.09), although its multiplier falls to 0.19–0.25; at η=0.03\eta=0.03 every method fails.

Appendix F Grokking test

The question is whether the loss spikes that accompany grokking with adaptive optimizers (Thilak et al., 2022) are needed for it. We trained the one-layer transformer of Nanda et al. (2023) on modular addition (p=113p=113, 30%30\% of pairs, full batch, 50,000 steps) with AdamW (weight decay 1) and with Adam without weight decay, using the five optimizers of the GPT study and three seeds each (Tables 10 and 14). With weight decay all 15 runs grokked, after 11.4k–21.9k steps. Clipping and the cubic map with k=1k=1 lowered the median of the largest training loss after memorization about fourfold (0.14 and 0.13 against 0.57 for AdamW; not on every seed) without a significant delay: the median steps to grok, 18.4k and 15.6k against 14.6k, lie within AdamW’s own seed range, and across runs the spike size shows no significant correlation with the time to grok (Spearman 0.22, p=0.43p=0.43). This spike measure, chosen after looking at the curves, extends to the end of training and so includes the time after grokking; restricted to the window before grokking, the correlation is positive (Spearman 0.50, p=0.06p=0.06, 15 runs): larger spikes went with later, not earlier, grokking, although part of this is mechanical, since a longer window tends to contain a larger maximum. The cubic map with k=4k=4 grokked earlier than AdamW on each of the three seeds (by 1.4k–2.4k steps), a difference that three seeds cannot establish. VRAdam’s damper reduced the spikes inconsistently. Without weight decay no run grokked (test accuracy at most 0.27), and there the maps produced the largest spikes of the study on some seeds (Table 10). In this setting, reducing the measured loss peaks did not consistently delay grokking, and the maps are not a reliable way to remove the peaks.

Basin experiments (Section 5): 300 initial conditions, 15,000 iterations (40,000 for β1≥0.95\beta_{1}\geq 0.95; runs with one tenth of the iterations give identical shares to two decimals); an orbit counts as reached when |yt+1+yt|<10−6​(1+|yt|)|y_{t+1}+y_{t}|<10^{-6}(1+|y_{t}|) over the last four iterates. The Legendre speed is computed by Newton’s method from the upper bound min⁡(z,z1/n)\min(z,z^{1/n}), which converges monotonically (residual <2×10−15<2\times 10^{-15} relative). In the exact quadratic a run counts as on the orbit when the alternation index is at least 0.990.99, |Reff−1|≤0.01|R_{\mathrm{eff}}-1|\leq 0.01 and the amplitude is within 10−310^{-3} of the closed form. Exact quadratic: integration in the eigenbasis of CC, which leaves the tensor norm and hence the map unchanged (checked against direct integration, relative difference 10−1210^{-12}). Delay study (Section 4): RR swept from 0.50.5 to 44, initial deviation 10−3​c10^{-3}c, 64 noise realizations per rate; peak ReffR_{\mathrm{eff}} is the maximum of R​gR\,g along the sweep; the linear estimate is the RR at which the propagated amplitude reaches half the orbit amplitude. Sensitivity at the ResNet rate: sweep to R=5R=5, initial deviations 10−610^{-6}–11 (in units of cc), cubic and quartic maps. Controlled ramps (Fig. 2): float64 throughout; pretraining 1,500 steps at R=0.5R=0.5 with η\eta reset from the top eigenvalue every 50 steps; power iteration warm-started from the previous eigenvector (200 iterations at the start of a ramp, then four every five steps); the two copies share the momentum at the kick; a run stops ten steps after |xt||x_{t}| first exceeds 100 times the exit threshold; at ρ=0.001\rho=0.001 the kick is δ=10−4\delta=10^{-4} so that the decayed deviation stays above the rounding level of the trajectory difference; noise is added to the gradient of the second copy only; the model distributions use 400 realizations on the measured path of each run. GPU studies: curvature computations in FP32 with TF32 disabled and deterministic cuDNN; training in FP32 for the full-batch studies and the grokking test, and with bf16 autocast for the minibatch ResNet-32, ResNet-18 and GPT studies (Table 12); Lanczos with full re-orthogonalization, eigenvalue-error and stagnation stopping, two independent starts for calibration.
